```{r}
#| message: false
#| echo: false
# Code to import data, for reference
library(tidyverse)
library(vroom)
library(broom)
# insurance.csv is from
# https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/d3lhomi10/medical-cost-personal-dataset
insurance_data <- vroom("insurance.csv") %>% 
  mutate(across(c(sex, smoker, region), as.factor))
insurance_fit <- lm(charges ~ ., data = insurance_data)
insurance_data$bmi_group <- as.factor(cut(
  insurance_data$bmi,
  breaks = c(0, 25, 30, Inf),
  labels = c("Normal", "Overweight", "Obese")
))

```

## Starting point

**AI system and date:** ChatGPT, 11/9/2026

> How is the amount spent on healthcare related to age, sex, BMI, number of children, smoking status, and region of the United States you live in? We are using a multiple linear regression model. The baseline result is that smoking, BMI, number of children, and age all are associated with significant changes in yearly healthcare charges. We wanted to see which predictors were the most important in predicting healthcare charges. Though we could use a best-subsets selection to get an idea of which matters most, we wanted to directly compare each variable's importance on the same baseline. A model selection search will tell us which variables should be included, but not rank and measure their importance.

For each, explain how it strengthens the same research question, how its result would enter the final case study, the implementation steps, and two ways I could verify it. Do not choose for me.

The extension must respond to your findings, improve the analysis or its communication, and appear substantively in the final case-study page. It cannot replace the baseline model or the two required STAT 330 elements, and it cannot shift the project away from the course’s regression focus. ## My decisions

- **Accepted:** We used ChatGPT's advice for what extension may work well. We used most of the advice it had for implementation and the code it gave us to create the permutation importance feature. We used the graphic and simulation it made to create the permutation feature.
- **Changed:** We adapted the code to be functional and relevant to our model. We added units to our graphics.
- **Rejected or corrected:** There was a bug in the code ChatGPT generated for us; it had used the keyword `repeat` as a variable name, which caused a syntax error. It created two "independent checks" for us as well, which we did not use because we wanted to check its work independently.  

**Connection to the final case study:** Our extension is in the section labeled "A new direction with AI" on the main report page. 

## Independent verification

1. If our extension shows that smoking, age, and BMI are substantially more important than the other predictors, than a best-subsets selection using BIC should hopefully select those same predictors. 
```{r}
bestglm::bestglm(
    insurance_data |> select(-bmi_group) |> as.data.frame(), 
    TopModels = 5,
    IC = "BIC"
)$BestModels
```

> This best-subsets BIC selection selects `age`, `bmi`, `children`, and `smoker`. This is some weak evidence that the AI's importance ranking is correct, as these are the top 4 predictors, but this best-subsets search does not rank the predictors in any way. This is why a best-subsets selection or other model selection method is not sufficient for ranking the importance of predictors, because the only information we get is if a variable should be included or not, whereas the AI's importance ranking assigns values to each predictor which we can use to rank and compare them. Because we only get a `TRUE` or `FALSE` for each predictor, we cannot say which matters most for prediction with a normal model selection search algorithm.

2. We can use $R^2$ to explore which variables are the most important. We can fit partial models, each one dropping one of our predictors, and see how much the $R^2$ decreases when we drop each variable. 

```{r}
partial1 <- lm(charges ~ . - age - bmi_group, data = insurance_data)
partial2 <- lm(charges ~ . - sex - bmi_group, data = insurance_data)
partial3<- lm(charges ~ . - bmi - bmi_group, data = insurance_data)
partial4 <- lm(charges ~ . - children - bmi_group, data = insurance_data)
partial5 <- lm(charges ~ . - smoker - bmi_group, data = insurance_data)
partial6 <- lm(charges ~ . - region - bmi_group, data = insurance_data)

adj.r.squareds <- c(
    glance(partial1)$adj.r.squared,
    glance(partial2)$adj.r.squared,
    glance(partial3)$adj.r.squared,
    glance(partial4)$adj.r.squared,
    glance(partial5)$adj.r.squared,
    glance(partial6)$adj.r.squared
)

results.chart <- tibble(
    `Dropped Predictor` = c("Age", "Sex", "BMI", "Children", "Smoker", "Region"),
    `Drop in adjusted R^2` = glance(insurance_fit)$adj.r.squared - adj.r.squareds
)
knitr::kable(results.chart)
```

This table lists the change in adjusted $R^2$, where a positive number means a drop in adjusted $R^2$. Omitting each of the variables caused a drop in adjusted $R^2$ except for sex, however the drop due to omitting region, children, and sex were all very small (<.003). This also reinforces the AI work, showing that age, BMI, and especially smoking status have a significant impact on the predictions. $R^2$ is also nice because it is quantifiable. The change in $R^2$ is the change in the percentage of variation that the model explains when we add that predictor. So, we can see that removing `smoker` causes the amount of variation explained to drop by nearly 63%, removing `age` and `bmi` cause the amount of explained variation to drop by about 9% and 3% respectively, while removing `sex`, `children`, or `region` cause a drop of less than .3% each, or even an increase in the case of `sex`. 

## Remaining limitation
One limitation that remains is that that correlation does not mean causation. We're modeling the impact of `sex`, `children`, `smoker`, `BMI`, `age`, and `region`, but there are other factors that could be impacting insurance pricing that the data doesn't show. An example of this could be previous medical history or disabilities that can influence the price. Even though the permutation importance simulation, the best-subsets selection using BIC, and the drop in $R^2$ all show that `smoker` can explain a lot of the variation in healthcare charges, we cannot conclude that healthcare charges are increased by smoking. 

## Other AI use, if any

We used AI to proofread. We also used it to debug code and understand errors in it. We also used it to help with the coding where appropriate, i.e. remembering how to code a lasso regression in R, how to make plots look nicer, etc.
